title: “LET YOUR CURSE FALL ON ME.” — THE MOTHER WHO HELPED HER SON STEAL A BLESSING… AND THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO LET DECEPTION HAVE THE FINAL WORD
paragraphs: “LET YOUR CURSE FALL ON ME.” — THE MOTHER WHO HELPED HER SON STEAL A BLESSING… AND THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO LET DECEPTION HAVE THE FINAL WORD

She knew her husband was about to bless the wrong son. She knew her plan was a lie. And when her frightened son warned her about the consequences, she spoke seven terrifying words: “Let your curse be on me.” What happened inside that family would tear a household apart, send a son running for his life, and reveal a truth many Christians still struggle to accept: God’s promises never need our sins to make them come true.
There are things a mother will do for her child that nobody else would dare to do.
She will sacrifice her sleep. Give away her last meal. Carry burdens she never speaks about. Pray through nights when everybody else has stopped believing.
But there is a dangerous moment when a mother's love becomes tangled with fear.
When protecting a child becomes controlling his future.
When believing God's promise turns into trying to force God's hand.
And when the desire to secure a blessing becomes so overwhelming that a person begins justifying the very sin that could destroy the family.
That is where we find Rebekah.
Not standing in a temple.
Not kneeling beside an altar.
Not offering a beautiful prayer.
She was listening to a conversation she was never meant to hear.
Her elderly husband, Isaac, was preparing to bless their older son, Esau.
And Rebekah was about to do something that would change her family forever.
She would help her younger son, Jacob, deceive his own father.
But what makes this story so disturbing is not simply that a mother encouraged deception.
It is what she said when her son became afraid.
“Upon me be thy curse, my son: only obey my voice.” — Genesis 27:13, KJV
Read that again.
She was willing to speak of bearing a curse rather than allow her preferred outcome to slip away.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of this story is that Rebekah was not a woman who knew nothing about God.
She had heard from Him.
She knew something about His promise.
Yet she still chose deception.
And before we condemn her too quickly, we need to ask a question that might expose something uncomfortable in our own hearts.
Have you ever believed God for something so deeply that you became willing to disobey Him to make it happen?
Maybe you never dressed your child in another person's clothes.
Maybe you never deceived a dying father.
But perhaps you manipulated a situation because you were afraid of losing someone.
Perhaps you hid the truth because you believed the truth would destroy what you were trying to protect.
Perhaps you prayed for God's will while quietly arranging everything to ensure your own will prevailed.
That is why Genesis 27 is not merely an ancient family scandal.
It is a mirror.
And sometimes the hardest part of reading Scripture is discovering that the person we are most disappointed in looks disturbingly like us.
Long before the deception, Rebekah had received a remarkable revelation.
During her pregnancy, when the children struggled within her, she inquired of the LORD.
God answered:

“Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23, KJV
The Hebrew conclusion is especially important:
וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר
Ve-rav ya'avod tsa'ir.
Commonly understood in this context as:
“And the older shall serve the younger.”
This was extraordinary.
In the ancient world, the firstborn son ordinarily enjoyed special privileges of inheritance and family standing.
But God had revealed that the expected order would be overturned.
Jacob, the younger twin, would have a significant place in God's covenant purposes.
Rebekah did not have to invent that promise.
God had spoken before either child was born.
But knowing what God has promised and trusting how God will accomplish it are two very different things.
And that distinction would become the fracture running through her entire household.
Years passed.
The boys grew.
Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the field.
Jacob was described as a quiet man dwelling in tents.
Isaac loved Esau, particularly enjoying the food he brought from hunting.
Rebekah loved Jacob.
Genesis 25:28 does not hide the division.
This was a family where parental favoritism had taken root.
And favoritism rarely stays confined to the heart.
Eventually, it finds a way into conversations, decisions, alliances, and wounds that children carry for years.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You grew up in a house where one child was celebrated and another was compared.
Where affection seemed easier for one sibling to receive.
Where approval had to be earned.
Where love was real, perhaps, but painfully unequal.
You may be an adult now, with children of your own, yet a sentence spoken at the dinner table decades ago still echoes inside you.
Genesis does not romanticize this family.
The patriarchs were not flawless heroes.
They were human beings living under the mercy of a faithful God.
And one day, their divided affections would collide with a divine promise.
Isaac was old, and his eyesight had become poor.
Believing his death might be approaching, he called Esau and asked him to hunt game and prepare the food he loved so that he might bless him.
Rebekah overheard.
She understood what was at stake.
And instead of seeking a truthful resolution, she moved immediately into action.
She summoned Jacob.
She instructed him to bring two young goats from the flock.
She would prepare the food Isaac enjoyed.
Jacob would carry it to his father.
And Isaac, unable to see clearly, would be led to believe that Jacob was Esau.
The plan was calculated.
The food.
The clothing.
The timing.
The disguise.
Every detail was designed to make a lie believable.
But Jacob noticed a problem.
His brother was hairy.
He was not.
What if Isaac touched him?
What if the deception was discovered?
Listen carefully to Jacob's objection.
“My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing.” — Genesis 27:12, KJV
Jacob was afraid.
But the text does not present his initial objection as a courageous refusal to lie.
He was concerned about being discovered and cursed.
That is an important distinction.
Sometimes we resist sin not because we hate what it is, but because we fear what will happen if somebody finds out.
We are afraid of exposure more than disobedience.
Afraid of consequences more than corruption.
Afraid of losing our reputation more than grieving the God who sees what is hidden.
Then Rebekah answered.
In Hebrew, Genesis 27:13 reads:
עָלַי קִלְלָתְךָ בְּנִי אַךְ שְׁמַע בְּקֹלִי
Alai qilelatekha beni, akh shema beqoli.
A close translation is:
“Upon me be your curse, my son; only listen to my voice.”
The Hebrew word קִלְלָה (qelalah) means a curse, the opposite of the blessing Jacob hoped to receive.
Rebekah was not uttering a magical formula that could guarantee the transfer of divine judgment from Jacob to herself.
She was declaring her willingness to take responsibility for the feared consequence and urging him to obey her instructions.
Notice the force of her final words.
Only listen to my voice.
That is the tragedy.
The woman who had once received the word of the LORD was now directing her son toward a lie.
And she was asking him to trust her voice.
There is a painful spiritual warning here.
Even people who know God's promises can begin listening more closely to their fears than to His truth.
Rebekah may have believed she was protecting the future God had revealed.
But the biblical narrative never presents her deception as a command from God.
A divine promise does not turn a dishonest method into a holy one.
A good outcome does not make every road toward it righteous.
And a mother's sincere concern does not make manipulation harmless.
That is a truth we need desperately in our generation.
We can call something protection when it is actually control.
We can call something wisdom when it is actually fear.
We can call something spiritual discernment when it is actually our refusal to surrender an outcome.
We can even say, “God told me,” when what we really mean is, “I cannot bear the possibility of things happening differently.”
And perhaps that is why this story hurts.
Because Rebekah's actions were not born in a world where God was absent.
They happened in a family that knew His covenant.
She had a promise.
But she did not trust God enough to leave its fulfillment in His hands.
Jacob followed her instructions.
Rebekah prepared the meal.
She dressed him in Esau's garments.
She placed the skins of the goats on his hands and the smooth part of his neck.
And then Jacob entered his father's presence.
Imagine the silence inside that room.
An elderly father.
A son wearing another man's clothes.
A blessing waiting to be spoken.
And a lie standing between them.
Isaac asked who had come.
Jacob answered:
“I am Esau thy firstborn.” — Genesis 27:19, KJV
It was false.
He was not Esau.
And the deception did not stop there.
When Isaac wondered how the game had been found so quickly, Jacob replied:
“Because the LORD thy God brought it to me.” — Genesis 27:20, KJV
Now the lie had become even darker.
Jacob invoked God's name to support a false story.
He used the language of providence to make deception sound believable.
That should disturb us.
Because one of the most dangerous things a person can do is attach God's name to something God never authorized.
We see versions of it today.
A person claims God approves of a relationship built on betrayal.
A leader uses spiritual language to silence legitimate questions.
A believer calls dishonesty a necessary sacrifice for ministry.
A parent pressures a child toward a decision and describes the pressure as God's will.
But God's name is not a shield for our manipulation.
And Scripture never teaches that the LORD requires us to lie in order to preserve His purposes.
Isaac remained suspicious.
He heard Jacob's voice.
But he felt what appeared to be Esau's hands.
“The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” — Genesis 27:22, KJV
What a devastating sentence.
The father sensed something was wrong.
But the disguise prevailed.
Jacob received the blessing.
The words were spoken.
And for a moment, the plan appeared to have succeeded.
But then Esau returned.
Carrying the meal he had prepared for his father.
Expecting the blessing he believed was waiting for him.
He entered the room.
And everything changed.
Isaac realized what had happened.
Genesis says he trembled exceedingly.
Esau cried out with a great and bitter cry.
The blessing had already been given.
His brother had deceived their father.
And the family was suddenly standing in the wreckage of its own choices.
Can you imagine that cry?
Not the cry of a man who had merely lost an argument.
The cry of someone who believed a defining part of his future had been taken from him.
Yet we must not erase the earlier part of Esau's story.
Genesis 25 records that he had sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal, treating it with contempt.
Hebrews 12:16–17 later warns readers through Esau's example.
Esau was not simply an innocent victim in every aspect of this family's history.
Neither was Jacob justified in deceiving Isaac.
Both truths matter.
Scripture is not asking us to excuse one person's sin because another person also sinned.
It is showing us a household where several people made destructive choices, while God's covenant purpose remained greater than their failures.
And then came the consequences.
Esau hated Jacob.
He planned to kill him after their father's death.
Rebekah learned of the threat and urged Jacob to flee to her brother Laban.
The son she had worked so desperately to secure a blessing for now had to leave home.
Think about that.
She wanted to protect his future.
But her plan helped create the circumstances that drove him away.
She wanted him blessed.
But she could not keep him safe from the anger that followed.
She wanted to hold on to what God had promised.
And she watched the son she loved depart.
Genesis does not explicitly say that Rebekah never saw Jacob again, and it does not tell us when she died.
We should not pretend to know what Scripture leaves unrecorded.
But we do know that Jacob's departure brought painful separation, and the narrative does not record a later reunion between mother and son.
That silence is heartbreaking enough.
Because there are victories that do not feel like victories once we see what they cost.
There are arguments we win while relationships collapse.
There are outcomes we secure while trust disappears.
There are things we obtain through manipulation that we later wish we had entrusted to God.
And there is a question worth asking before we make our next desperate decision.
What if the thing you are trying so hard to control is the very thing God is asking you to surrender?
Perhaps you are a mother afraid for your child.
You have watched him make decisions that frighten you.
You have prayed until your words feel exhausted.
You want him protected from every mistake, every heartbreak, every consequence.
And somewhere along the way, your concern has begun turning into pressure.
You keep arranging things.
Interfering.
Deciding.
Trying to rescue him from every uncomfortable lesson.
Not because you do not love him.
But because you love him and are terrified of what might happen if you stop controlling everything.
Rebekah's story is not a command to stop caring for your children.
It is a warning that love must remain accountable to truth.
A mother can pray.
Guide.
Correct.
Warn.
Protect where protection is needed.
But she cannot become her child's savior.
That place belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
And perhaps you are not the parent in this story.
Perhaps you are Jacob.
You have spent years wearing a version of yourself that you thought would finally earn someone's approval.
You learned to say what people wanted to hear.
You learned to hide what might disappoint them.
You became skilled at looking confident while feeling terrified of being discovered.
You entered rooms pretending to be somebody else because you believed the real you would never be enough.
Jacob wore his brother's clothes to obtain his father's blessing.
How many people today are still wearing someone else's identity to feel worthy of love?
A borrowed personality.
A manufactured success.
A carefully edited life.
A religious appearance that conceals a weary soul.
You smile in church while silently struggling.
You post Bible verses while wrestling with private guilt.
You tell people you are doing well because explaining the truth feels too painful.
But here is something the Gospel wants you to hear.
Jesus Christ did not come to save the person you pretend to be. He came to save sinners who need His mercy.
You do not have to deceive Him into accepting you.
You cannot hide your sins from Him.
And you do not need to manufacture a spotless history before coming to Him in repentance and faith.
He already knows.
The lies.
The compromises.
The hidden fears.
The things you regret.
The choices you wish you could undo.
And still, the Gospel announces that forgiveness is available through His death and resurrection.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because deception is acceptable.
But because Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Yet the story of Jacob does not end in Genesis 27.
That is where the deeper beauty begins.
The deceiver became a fugitive.
The son who had obtained a blessing through disguise found himself sleeping under the open sky with a stone for a pillow.
In Genesis 28, God appeared to Jacob in a dream at Bethel.
The LORD reaffirmed the covenant promises associated with Abraham and Isaac.
And He said:
“And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest.” — Genesis 28:15, KJV
Do not miss the wonder of that moment.
Jacob was not standing there with a spotless record.
He was leaving behind a fractured home.
Yet God was faithful to His covenant.
This was grace.
Not approval of Jacob's deception.
Not permission to continue sinning.
Grace.
The undeserved kindness of a God who does not abandon His purposes when human beings reveal how desperately they need Him.
But God's faithfulness did not mean Jacob would avoid hardship.
He would experience years of difficult service.
He would be deceived by Laban, his own relative.
He would face conflict, fear, uncertainty, and the painful consequences of life in a broken world.
The man who had manipulated his father would learn what it felt like to be manipulated himself.
And eventually, he would face something he had spent years avoiding.
His past.
In Genesis 32, as Jacob prepared to meet Esau again, he was afraid.
He had possessions.
A family.
Years of experience.
But the memory of his brother's anger still stood before him.
That night, Jacob wrestled with a mysterious man until daybreak.
The encounter culminated in a divine blessing and a new name.
“Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.” — Genesis 32:28, KJV
The Hebrew name יַעֲקֹב (Ya'aqov), Jacob, is associated in Genesis with the heel and with supplanting.
The name יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisra'el), Israel, is explained in this passage in relation to striving with God and prevailing.
The precise linguistic history of the names is complex, but the narrative's spiritual significance is unmistakable.
God gave Jacob a new name at a decisive moment of encounter.
And the man who had once entered his father's room pretending to be his brother now had to answer a question about his own identity.
“What is thy name?” — Genesis 32:27, KJV
“Jacob.”
This time, he did not say, “Esau.”
He gave his own name.
We should not reduce this profound encounter to a simple lesson about admitting one's identity, because the passage is far richer than that.
But the contrast is striking.
In Genesis 27, Jacob had claimed to be someone else.
In Genesis 32, he stood before the divine encounter as Jacob.
And God named him Israel.
There is something beautiful here for every person who has lived behind a mask.
The road toward transformation does not begin with pretending that your past never happened.
It begins with coming into the light.
Not to earn grace.
But to stop hiding from the God who gives it.
And when Jacob finally met Esau in Genesis 33, the reunion was not the bloodshed he had feared.
Esau ran to meet him.
He embraced him.
They wept.
The story does not tell us that every future tension between their descendants disappeared.
But it does show a remarkable moment of reconciliation between two brothers whose relationship had been devastated by sin.
The family scandal did not have the final word.
God was still at work.
And now we come to something even greater than Jacob's story.
Because Genesis does not ultimately exist to make us admire Jacob.
It leads us through the covenant promises toward Jesus Christ.
God promised Abraham that through his offspring the nations would be blessed.
That covenant line continued through Isaac and Jacob.
And the New Testament directs our attention to Christ as the fulfillment of God's saving promise.
Galatians 3:16 identifies Christ as the promised offspring in whom the blessing reaches its fulfillment.
Through Jesus, salvation is offered not only to one family or nation, but to people from every nation who believe.
And here the contrast becomes breathtaking.
Rebekah said to Jacob:
“Upon me be your curse.”
Centuries later, the apostle Paul wrote concerning Jesus:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.” — Galatians 3:13, KJV
The Greek text includes these words:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”
The verb ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) expresses redemption, a buying out or release from bondage.
The word κατάρας (kataras) means curse.
And Paul's statement is not merely that Jesus sympathized with cursed people.
It is that Christ redeemed His people from the law's curse by bearing it on their behalf.
But we must be careful with this comparison.
Rebekah's words and Christ's sacrifice are not the same kind of act.
Rebekah offered to bear a feared curse while encouraging a deception.
Jesus, the sinless Son of God, willingly bore the curse associated with our violation of God's law.
Rebekah's declaration did not redeem Jacob from sin.
Christ's sacrifice truly redeems those who belong to Him.
Rebekah's plan depended on disguise.
Christ's saving work was accomplished through perfect obedience.
Rebekah sought to secure a blessing by wrongdoing.
Jesus secured our redemption through His righteousness, His sacrificial death, and His victorious resurrection.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why the cross is so much more than a religious symbol.
It is where the seriousness of our sin and the astonishing mercy of God meet.
Jesus did not merely teach us how to become better people.
He came to rescue sinners who could not rescue themselves.
The One who never lied suffered for liars.
The One who never manipulated suffered for manipulators.
The One who never betrayed the Father suffered for those who had turned away from Him.
As 2 Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
That does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
It means the sinless Christ stood in the place of sinners in God's saving purpose.
And through Him, those who believe are reconciled to God.
Think about the difference.
Jacob approached his father wearing another man's garments and falsely claiming another man's identity.

The believer approaches the heavenly Father through faith in Jesus Christ, not by deceiving Him, but because Christ has truly provided the righteousness and reconciliation we could never produce for ourselves.
There is no fraud in the Gospel.
There is a Savior.
There is a cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
And there is new life for those who belong to Christ.
This is what makes grace so astonishing.
God does not declare deception righteous.
He saves deceivers and calls them to walk in truth.
He does not call manipulation love.
He transforms hearts so that love can become sincere.
He does not erase the moral seriousness of our past.
He provides forgiveness and teaches us how to live differently.
Perhaps that is the word someone reading this has needed for years.
You cannot undo every choice you made.
You cannot retrieve every word spoken in anger.
You cannot travel backward and become the parent you wish you had been.
You cannot erase the years you spent pretending.
You may still have consequences to face.
You may need to apologize.
Confess.
Make restitution where possible.
Seek reconciliation without demanding that wounded people trust you immediately.
But your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Jesus Christ still receives sinners who turn to Him.
And His grace does more than comfort us.
It changes us.
If you are a mother who has been trying to control every detail of your child's life, perhaps your prayer tonight needs to change.
Not merely, “Lord, make my child do what I want.”
But, “Lord, teach me to love my child without trying to take Your place.”
If you are a father whose favoritism has wounded your family, perhaps the next faithful step is not another explanation.
Perhaps it is an apology.
If you are a son or daughter who has built a life around gaining approval, perhaps it is time to stop wearing the clothes of someone you were never created to be.
If you have been using religious language to justify something you know is wrong, perhaps this is the moment to repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not when everything becomes convenient.
Now.
Because the Gospel does not invite us to decorate our chains with Bible verses.
It invites us to be set free.
And there is a particular kind of freedom that comes when you finally stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
You do not have to keep calling fear wisdom.
You do not have to keep calling control protection.
You do not have to keep calling compromise faith.
You can tell the truth.
You can come to Christ.
You can begin again.
Not because you are strong enough to rewrite your own story.
But because Jesus is mighty to save.
And perhaps you have been reading all this with tears in your eyes because you know exactly where your life began to unravel.
You remember the decision.
The conversation.
The lie.
The day you chose what seemed easiest instead of what was right.
You remember the people it hurt.
You remember who you were before it happened.
And some nights you wonder whether God could still do anything beautiful with a life carrying so much regret.
Look at Jacob.
Not as proof that our sins have no consequences.
But as testimony that God's mercy is greater than the failures of those He calls.
Look beyond Jacob to Christ.
Because the hope of the Christian is not that every family scandal will receive a perfect earthly resolution.
Some relationships remain difficult.
Some wounds take years to heal.
Some consequences remain even after repentance.
Our hope is deeper than the promise of an easy ending.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Jesus.
The One who can forgive.
The One who can restore fellowship with God.
The One who can teach us to walk in truth after years of deception.
The One who can sustain us when reconciliation is incomplete.
The One who can take what sin has disfigured and begin the patient work of renewal.
From scandal to grace does not mean the scandal was good. It means the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than the scandal.
And that is the message Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim.
Not that every believer has a perfect testimony.
Not that faithful people never fall.
Not that Christianity is a life without tears.
But that Jesus Christ is worthy of our trust, our repentance, our obedience, and our worship.
We need this truth in a world overflowing with religious noise.
We need Scripture that is read carefully, not twisted to flatter us.
We need discipleship that does more than produce emotional moments.
We need a faith that survives when the excitement fades and obedience becomes costly.
That is why Gospel Warrior continues sharing Scripture-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, and resources designed to help people grow deeper in Christ.
These resources are offered to encourage believers, strengthen families, equip seekers, and help people become more grounded in the Word of God.
And not because every Christian is required to give to this particular work.
But because voluntary, cheerful generosity is one meaningful way believers can participate in spreading the Gospel.
Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the biblical spirit of Christian giving.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a transaction for divine favor.
But love expressing itself through willing generosity.
Some believers may choose to give from the portion of their budget they set aside for offerings or Christian ministry.
The purpose is simple.
To help sustain and expand this work so that more people can encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel, find discipleship resources, and be encouraged to follow Jesus Christ.
The exhausted mother reading Scripture after midnight.
The young man fighting a secret addiction.
The father trying to rebuild trust with his children.
The believer who has drifted from church and is searching for a way back.
We cannot promise what any individual reader will do with the message.
But we can faithfully keep pointing people toward the Savior.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for reflection, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about Jesus.
It is the opportunity to participate in a ministry whose central message is that Christ still saves, forgives, restores, and transforms.
Not simply to increase a number on a screen.
But because someone in your circle may be silently carrying the weight of a family mistake.
Someone may believe that their failures have disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone may be making a decision right now that fear is disguising as faith.
And perhaps a Scripture-centered message shared at the right moment will encourage them to open their Bible, repent, seek help, or turn to Jesus.
Not to expose their private struggles.
Not to embarrass them.
But to encourage them with the truth that no one needs to keep hiding behind a false identity before God.
You do not have to disclose details you are not comfortable sharing.
Your testimony may encourage another reader to take an honest step toward Christ.
For the days when obedience feels slower than compromise.
For the moments when you need to remember that God's promises are not dependent on your ability to manipulate circumstances.
Because what matters most is not whether people remember the name of a ministry.
It is whether they come to know, trust, and follow the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now return with me, one final time, to that room in Genesis 27.
An old father sits in darkness.
A son stands before him wearing another man's clothes.
A mother waits for a blessing she has tried to secure through deception.
Outside that room, a brother is coming home.
And none of them fully understands the pain that is about to unfold.
The mother says, “Let your curse be on me.”
The son lies.
The father blesses.
The brother weeps.
The family fractures.
And the deceiver runs.
If the story ended there, it would be a tragedy of human failure.
But God was not finished.
Years later, Jacob would encounter the LORD, receive a new name, and continue as a bearer of the covenant promise.
And generations later, from the covenant line God preserved, Jesus Christ would come.
Not to help sinners hide their guilt.
But to bear sin's judgment and bring redemption.
Not to teach us how to steal a blessing.
But to give, by grace, what we could never earn.
Not to make deception acceptable.
But to set us free to walk in truth.
Rebekah tried to secure a future through a lie.
Jesus opened the way to eternal life through His perfect obedience, death, and resurrection.
And that is where this story must leave us.
Not worshiping Rebekah's determination.
Not excusing Jacob's dishonesty.
Not imagining that God needs our wrongdoing to fulfill His Word.
But bowing before the Savior whose faithfulness is greater than our failures.
So stop trying to force the blessing.
Stop hiding behind the disguise.
Stop asking God to approve what He is calling you to confess.
Come to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Trust His grace.
Follow His Word.
And remember this when your past whispers that your story is beyond redemption:
The clothes Jacob wore could fool his earthly father, but the sins you carry cannot fool your heavenly Father—and in Jesus Christ, you do not have to hide to be received.
